Read About Playa del Carmen

A Maya canoe launch turned ferry town turned the busiest resort strip on the Riviera Maya, in under fifty years.

From fishing village to ferry town

Long before Playa del Carmen had a name a foreigner could spell, it was Xaman-Ha, "waters of the north" in Yucatec Maya, a modest coastal settlement where pilgrims loaded canoes for the crossing to Cozumel, the island shrine of the goddess Ixchel. Three small groups of those Post-Classic structures still stand in the Playacar neighborhood today, wedged between condominium walls and golf-course fairways, the oldest surviving evidence that this stretch of coast has always been a point of departure rather than a destination in itself.

The modern town traces to 1902, when the area was folded into the newly created territory of Quintana Roo, but it stayed a sleepy fishing settlement for most of the twentieth century — a handful of families, a church, and little else. The turn came in the early-to-mid 1970s, when a ferry dock was built to carry passengers and goods across to Cozumel, at the time the more developed of the two. The dock made Playa reachable rather than remote, and by the 1980s what had been a village of a few hundred people was absorbing the overflow of a booming Cancún tourist corridor sixty kilometers north.

A town built to launch canoes to Cozumel became, a century later, the place travelers pass through to get everywhere else on this coast.

Growth from there was less a wave than a flood: by the 1990s Playa del Carmen was among the fastest-growing municipalities in Mexico, and the population has since passed 300,000 permanent residents, up from a village of a few hundred within living memory. Fifth Avenue, the pedestrian spine that now runs several kilometers parallel to the beach, was a sand track as recently as the 1980s.

A hub, not a headline attraction

What makes Playa unusual among Mexican resort towns is that almost none of the region's marquee experiences are actually in it. Xcaret, the eco-archaeological park built around the ruins of the ancient Maya port of Polé, sits a half-hour drive south. Tulum's cliffside ruins and Cobá's Nohoch Mul — at 42 meters the tallest Maya structure in the northern Yucatán, reopened to climbers in December 2025 after a six-year closure — are further inland and south again. The cenotes that draw snorkelers and cave divers from across the world are scattered through the jungle in between.

Playa's role is logistical as much as scenic: a walkable base with an airport-adjacent highway, a functioning downtown, and, since March 2024, a station on the Tren Maya, the passenger rail line that now links the coast to Tulum in under an hour and reaches as far as Mérida and the inland ruins without a rental car. The town absorbs the visitor traffic so the archaeological sites and reserves around it don't have to.

Living with the reef, and the seaweed

The coast here sits inside the Mesoamerican Reef system, the second-largest barrier reef on Earth, which is both the reason Akumal's bay half an hour south was declared a marine turtle refuge in 2016 and the reason the region's ecology has become a visible, sometimes inconvenient part of the travel experience. Since the early 2010s, seasonal blooms of sargassum — a free-floating brown seaweed whose surge has been linked to nutrient runoff and shifting Atlantic currents — have washed onto Riviera Maya beaches most heavily between April and October, worst in June and July. Playa's town beach takes more of it than the sheltered leeward coast of Cozumel, a 45-minute ferry ride from the foot of Fifth Avenue and, for exactly that reason, still the closer swim on a bad seaweed week.

None of this has slowed the town down. Playa del Carmen remains what it has been since that first ferry dock went in: the coast's working front door, built for people on their way to somewhere else, that turned out to be worth stopping in for its own sake too.
